extracted.intended_audience: general literate public / readers of a 19th-century periodical (interested in theatre, fine arts, botany, and miscellany)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted criteria and practical guidance embedded in a 19th‑century magazine issue covering theatre history, art exhibition reviews, botanical practicalities, and miscellany. The page is a mixed-content periodical rather than an explicit modern rubric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre safety / egress
rubrics_metrics.description: The Globe theatre 'had only two doors' and narrow exits, which was noted as a cause of danger during the 1613 fire; narrow doors impeded escape and led to casualties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of multiple and sufficiently wide exits is implied as a safety requirement; thatched roofs and limited egress are cited as hazards (example: 'it was a great marvaile and a fair grace of God that the people had so little harm, having but two narrow doors to get out').

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre roofing / fire risk (material choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Thatched roofs and combustible stage dressings contributed to the rapid burning of the Globe ('some of the paper or other stuff ... did light on the thatch ... it kindled inwardly, and ran round like a train, consuming within less than an hour the whole house').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid highly combustible roofing and scenery; pay attention to ignition sources used for effects (e.g., cannon effects) and to materials used in stage decoration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seating arrangement & classed accommodation
rubrics_metrics.description: Theatres had galleries on three sides, 'rooms' under the lowest acting as boxes, and a yard resembling the modern pit where the 'groundlings' stood; different areas had different prices and social composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design of seating (galleries, boxes, pit/yard) determines audience type and experience; ticket tiers and physical arrangement should match intended demographic and viewing expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission pricing and accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Admission prices varied by location within the house: best rooms/boxes a shilling (later higher), galleries/some scaffolds sixpence, meaner playhouses one penny or two pence; spectators paid at multiple points ('one penny at the gate, another at the entrie of the scaffold, and a third for quiet standing').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pricing structure can be multi-tiered and affects who attends; excessive or multiple small charges were customary historically and shaped audience behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre capacity estimation via receipts
rubrics_metrics.description: Receipts for a day's performance (e.g., '20_l_. was the greatest receipt for one day's performance') were used to infer house capacity (approx. 700 persons estimated from receipts and ticket prices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Box-office receipts and ticket pricing provide practical metrics for estimating venue capacity and commercial success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target audience influences repertoire and refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Some exhibitions/performances were 'calculated for the lower class of people' and were less refined; proximity to bear-baiting and popular sports suggested a less refined audience for the Globe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the tone, content, and staging of performances to the expected audience; nearby entertainments and social milieu influence the refinement and subject-matter appropriate for a venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/topographical accuracy for theatre description
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of Bankside and historic playhouses include specific place-names (Globe Alley, Pike Garden, Cardinal's Hat Court) and surviving traces (Winchester Square) as important to reconstructing past theatre locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When documenting historic theatres, include surviving toponyms, physical traces, and documentary references (letters, registers) to support claims about site and usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrait painting — likeness and expression
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful portrait is judged by likeness and the expression of features: e.g., 'Cardinal Weld; a well painted portrait ... The features are dignified and finely intellectual.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate portraits on fidelity of likeness, appropriate expression conveying character, and how well the sitter's qualities (dignity, intellect, etc.) are rendered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting — colouring and flesh-tint execution
rubrics_metrics.description: Colouring and flesh-tint quality are singled out: 'A Philosopher ... Admirably coloured: the flesh tints and deep expression of the features will not escape notice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess technical handling of colour and flesh tones; naturalistic, well-modulated colouration and convincing flesh tints are markers of high execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition & subject depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Works are evaluated for composition and how successfully they present their subject (examples: 'A scene of beautiful repose', 'The Grecian Choirs ... the splendour of which is enhanced by the brightness of a summer's morning').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider compositional arrangement, harmony, mood, and fidelity to the source/idea (poem, history) when judging figurative or landscape painting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic/poetic fidelity in works derived from literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Several paintings are described as derived from lines by poets (Mrs. Hemans, Petrarch, Scott); the review notes how effectively the visual work evokes the quoted literary lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When art illustrates literary sources, evaluate how well it translates the text's imagery and tone into visual terms and whether the painting enhances or misrepresents the source material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral or thematic judgement in subject choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral assessment of subject matter is applied (e.g., 'a gaming-house furnishes an epitome of all the bad passions that rankle in the human breast' — the painting's subject is used to comment on human vice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics may judge works not only on formal qualities but on the moral/social message of the subject; subject matter that illuminates vice or virtue can be praised or critiqued accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Execution and finish — frame and presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame and finish are assessed alongside the picture: 'The framework is excellent, and well appointed for St. James's, Windsor, or Buckingham Palace. We hope the picture will be liked there as well as the frame.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical presentation (frame, finish) contributes to a work's suitability for display and institutional patronage; critics note when framing appears superior to the painting itself as a negative sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portraits as instruments of status
rubrics_metrics.description: Portraits perpetuate authority: 'there is nothing like a portrait to perpetuate your brief authority' (noting portraits of ex-sheriffs and the Lord Chancellor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how a portrait functions socially — commemorative or status-reinforcing portraits may be judged for ceremonial appropriateness as well as likeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibition success metrics — sales, commissions, patron attendance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Society's success is measured by sales and commissions ('works ... to the amount of £18,000 ... have been sold' and 'numerous commissions given'), and public attendance at private view ('full attendance ... crowded with the carriages of visiters' and presence of nobility, patrons of art).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial sales, commissions, and attendance by influential patrons are used as practical indicators of an exhibition's success and the Society's effectiveness in promoting artists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality / works of imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: The review laments that 'Works of imagination are scarce' and notes a trend for empainting poetic/romantic ideas becoming fashionable (possibly to the detriment of originality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value originality and imaginative invention in art; scarcity of genuinely imaginative works is seen as a negative for an exhibition culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical seed handling — keep seeds dry before sowing
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Why should seeds be uniformly kept dry before sown?' — Because the least damp will cause an attempt at vegetation, when the seeds necessarily die, as the process cannot, as they are situated, go on.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Store seeds dry to avoid pre-germination; even slight damp can trigger germination and ruin seed viability prior to planting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watering regime for newly sown seeds
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Why, in summer, is continued watering required to newly sown seeds?' — Because ... the radicle which projects will wither away in parching weather if not supplied continuously with moisture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistent soil moisture after sowing in hot/dry conditions to support radicle establishment; single watering at sowing is insufficient in summer heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection for improving seed stock
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Why is selection important for procuring abundance of genuine seeds?' — Because we may then choose the most vigorous plants, which naturally prove of greater fecundity.' (example: one wheat plant producing 2,473 grains then used to produce substantially more seed over years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the most vigorous, fecund plants for seed production to increase yield and maintain seed quality across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of plant internal heat and observation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that plants possess internal heat detectable by thermometer ('Mr. Hunter appears to have detected this heat by a thermometer applied in frosty weather to the internal parts of vegetables newly opened').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use direct observation and appropriate instruments (thermometer) to detect physiological properties in plants; empirical measurement is presented as a proper method for botanical claims.
